description: The OAuth 2.1 / OpenID Connect client for ASP.NET Core applications. One call in Program.cs plus an Authority and a ClientId, and [Authorize] works. It configures ASP.NET Core's own OpenID Connect and cookie handlers rather than hand-rolling the protocol, so PKCE, state, nonce, JWKS rollover and token refresh come from the framework. Also provides the flows outside interactive sign-in: a setup probe that checks local configuration against the provider's live metadata, the client credentials grant, and dynamic client registration (RFC 7591/7592). Built for Ark.oAuth.Oidc, but because it is the stock handler underneath, changing Authority and ClientId points the same application at Entra ID, Okta, Auth0 or Keycloak.
releaseNotes:
2.4.6 — security fixes. No API is removed or renamed and nothing has to be configured, but some
requests that used to pass are now refused:

* **An API that was given no Audience now checks one.** AddArkOidcApi expects the audience the provider
  publishes for the tenant's access tokens (ark_access_token_audience, published from this release of
  Ark.oAuth.Oidc). A token addressed to one agent (A2A) or one MCP endpoint used to be accepted by every
  such API. Against an older provider the audience is still not checked, but a token carrying `act` is
  refused. ark_oauth_client:Audience works as before. JwtBearerOptions.Audience set afterwards now
  decides (it had no effect without it), and so does TokenValidationParameters.ValidateAudience = false.
* **Roles follow the token.** ark_claims are read again each time the session's tokens are refreshed, so
  a claim taken away stops being a role then. It used to last as long as the session.
* **The access check runs again with each refresh.** With AccountSwitch:RequireArkClaims or
  OnEvaluateAccess, an account that has lost its access is signed out; a handler that throws there signs
  out too. OnEvaluateAccess is therefore called more often than once per sign-in.
* **One refresh per refresh token.** Requests that arrive together near expiry share one, where all but
  the first used to sign the user out and revoke the family. Signing out drops what it produced.
* **The flows beside the sign-in make its checks.** ArkClientCredentials, ArkRegistration and
  ArkAgentTokens need https unless the authority is loopback or RequireHttpsMetadata is off, and an
  issuer that is the authority (compared without case). An Authority that only reaches the provider, and
  is not its issuer, still signs in but is refused here. The client's HttpClient follows no redirects.
* **WithArkMaxAge is enforced.** A sign-in whose ID token says the user authenticated longer ago fails at
  the callback (AuthErrorPath), as it does in the Node and Python clients.
* **GetArkAgentTokenAsync uses the session first.** A request authenticated by its cookie acts for that
  user whatever Authorization header came with it; one a bearer token authenticated, for the bearer.
* AddArkAgentApi requires typ at+jwt whatever RequireAccessTokenTypeHeader says: the client's own ID
  tokens carry the same audience. Request.ArkUser() reads no cookie outside UseLegacyFlow.

The provider, Ark.oAuth.Oidc, is itself an MCP server in this release, with which an agent sets it up and
administers it. The client and the provider can be upgraded in either order.

2.4.2 — agent-to-agent (A2A). Additive; nothing existing changes.

* **ArkAgentTokens** (registered by AddArkOidcClient): GetTokenAsync(audience) returns a token
  addressed to another agent, as this client itself; GetTokenAsync(audience, subjectToken) returns
  one on behalf of a user (token exchange, RFC 8693). Cached until shortly before expiry.
  GetAgentCardSecurityAsync() fetches the security section of an A2A Agent Card.
* **AddArkAgentApi(config)**: AddArkOidcApi that accepts only tokens whose audience is this
  application's own ClientId.
* **User.ArkActors()**: the agents acting for the caller, from the token's `act` claim.
* **HttpContext.GetArkAgentTokenAsync(audience)**: a token for the next agent on behalf of whoever
  this request is from.
Needs a provider with A2A (Ark.oAuth.Oidc next release); see A2A.md in that package.

2.4.1 — published alongside Ark.oAuth.Oidc 2.4.1. No change to this package.

The code, API, options, defaults and dependencies are those of 2.4.0. The provider's 2.4.1 adds
webhooks, an opt-in module a host turns on with AddArkWebhooks(), and changes nothing on the wire,
so the app and the provider can be upgraded in either order. There is nothing to do when you
upgrade.

2.4.0 — published alongside Ark.oAuth.Oidc 2.4.0. No change to this package.

The code, API, options, defaults and dependencies are those of 2.3.0. The provider's 2.4.0 is built
to hold 30,000 signed-in users and to run on more than one instance, and changes nothing on the
wire, so the app and the provider can be upgraded in either order. There is nothing to do when you
upgrade.

2.3.0 — .NET 10, alongside Ark.oAuth.Oidc 2.3.0. No API change.

.NET 9 left support on 2026-11-10; .NET 10 is the long-term support release. The package moves onto
it with no change to its API, options, defaults or behaviour. It works with any Ark IdP the 2.2.x
client did, and the provider changes nothing on the wire in 2.3.0, so the app and the provider can
be upgraded in either order.

Before upgrading:
* **Move the app to .NET 10 first.** Target net10.0, build with the .NET 10 SDK and run on the
  ASP.NET Core 10 runtime. A net9.0 app fails restore with NU1202. An app that stays on net9.0 stays
  on 2.2.1, the last net9.0 release.
* **If the app pins Microsoft.IdentityModel.* itself**, raise those pins to 8.23.0 or remove them.
  A split graph builds, then fails at the first challenge with "Cannot redirect to the authorization
  endpoint".
* ASP.NET Core 10 answers 401/403 instead of redirecting on API endpoints. What this package does is
  unchanged: a challenge still goes to the OpenID Connect handler, and a signed-in user who is
  refused is still sent to the access-denied page by this package's own handler.

Version updates:
* Target framework: net9.0 → net10.0.
* Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.OpenIdConnect and Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer:
  8.0.15 → 10.0.15.
* Microsoft.IdentityModel.JsonWebTokens, Microsoft.IdentityModel.Protocols.OpenIdConnect and
  System.IdentityModel.Tokens.Jwt: 8.8.0 → 8.23.0, still one version across the graph.

2.2.1 — 2.2.0 republished through the release workflow. The published files differ from 2.2.0 only
in the version number.

2.2.0 — security release, alongside Ark.oAuth.Oidc 2.2.0. Upgrade both.

Behaviour changes:
* **AddArkOidcApi accepts only access tokens.** A token's header must declare typ at+jwt
  (RFC 9068), which Ark puts on every access token. Before this, an ID token, which every SPA
  holds, was accepted as an access token. If you use a provider that does not type its access
  tokens, set ark_oauth_client:RequireAccessTokenTypeHeader=false.
* **The v1 client routes are gone unless ark_oauth_client:UseLegacyFlow is set.** ClientController
  is an application part, so it used to answer in every MVC host that referenced this package.
  Its callback printed stack traces, and its /config route returned this configuration section,
  client secret included, to any signed-in user. /config is removed entirely.

Fixed:
* The ArkAuthContext user_info no longer reads its user, IP or claims from the ark_oauth_* cookies
  outside the legacy flow. Only v1 writes those cookies, so anything in them came from the browser.
* The ArkClientCredentials token cache is keyed on the client secret too (hashed). Before this, a
  caller with the right client_id and a wrong secret got another caller's token.
* AuthClientHelper escapes every value it puts in the onboarding URL.

Still owed by your API: authorise by Ark claims and check the caller's client_id. Every client of a
tenant shares one access-token audience.

2.1.0 — account switching on a shared browser.

Fixes the case where two people use one browser. Single sign-on is browser-wide, so once the first
person has signed in anywhere, the provider's session answers the authorize request of every other
client in that browser. The second person opens a different application, is silently signed in as
the first, is told they do not have access — and has no way back, because the sign-in link returns
to the same session and gives the same answer.

* ark_oauth_client:AccountSwitch:RequireArkClaims moves the entitlement check to the callback. An
  account with no ark_claims for this client is refused before the authentication cookie is
  written, so the browser never holds a session for somebody who cannot use the application.
* A built-in access-denied page at /ark/no-access names the account that is signed in and offers
  "Sign in as a different user", which challenges with prompt=login so the provider draws its
  sign-in form instead of answering from its session. It also replaces the framework's
  /Account/AccessDenied default for ordinary [Authorize] 403s, which most applications never
  create and which therefore renders as a 404.
* HttpContext.ArkSwitchUserAsync / ArkSignOutEverywhereAsync / ArkSignOutLocallyAsync, and
  ArkChallengeProperties.SwitchUser for a challenge you issue yourself — prompt, login_hint and
  max_age now reach the authorize request through the authentication properties.
* An AddArkOidcClient(configuration, options) overload carrying ArkClientEvents: OnEvaluateAccess
  for an entitlement rule of your own, OnAccessDenied to log it or render your own page.

The page and its two POST endpoints register themselves, so Program.cs needs no edit. Every part is
off or unchanged by default: consumers on 2.0.3 who set nothing get identical behaviour except that
an [Authorize] 403 now reaches an explanation instead of a 404.

2.0.3 — version alignment.

No API change over 2.0.2. Rebuilt and republished alongside Ark.oAuth.Oidc 2.0.3 so the two halves
carry the same version. Consumers on 2.0.2 can upgrade with no code change; the notes for the
earlier versions apply unchanged and are kept below.

Worth knowing if you are upgrading the provider at the same time: 2.0.3 of Ark.oAuth.Oidc adds
back-channel logout, and this package does not host the receiving endpoint. An application that
wants its own cookie dropped when the IdP session ends registers a backchannel_logout_uri and
implements that endpoint itself — validate the posted logout_token against the provider's JWKS
(typ "logout+jwt", matching iss and aud, an events claim, no nonce), end the session it names, and
answer 200 or 204. Applications that register no URI are unaffected and keep behaving exactly as
they do on 2.0.2.

2.0.2 — version alignment.

No API change over 2.0.1. Rebuilt and republished alongside Ark.oAuth.Oidc 2.0.2 so the two halves
carry the same version. Consumers on 2.0.1 can upgrade with no code change; the 2.0.1 and 2.0.0
notes apply unchanged and are kept below.

2.0.1 — maintenance release.

No API change over 2.0.0. Rebuilt and republished alongside Ark.oAuth.Oidc 2.0.1 to keep the two
halves on the same version, and to carry the packaging fixes below. Consumers on 2.0.0 can upgrade
with no code change; the 2.0.0 notes apply unchanged and are kept below.

Packaging: the package icon (ark_logo.png) and the readme are packed at the root of the .nupkg, so
nuget.org and the Visual Studio package manager show both. The icon is referenced through
PackageIcon rather than the deprecated PackageIconUrl, and is included with an empty PackagePath so
it lands at the package root on a non-Windows build too.

2.0.0 — the standards release.

* AddArkOidcClient now configures ASP.NET Core's OpenID Connect and cookie handlers against the
  provider's discovery document. Real PKCE, state and nonce validation, JWKS rollover and silent
  refresh all come from the framework instead of being hand-rolled.
* Authority and ClientId are the only required settings — no pasted rsaPublic, no issuer/audience
  to mirror, no per-tenant key table to keep in step with rotation.
* AddArkOidcApi for protecting an API with bearer tokens from the same provider.
* Ark authorization claims (ark_claims) are projected onto the principal as role claims, so
  [Authorize(Roles = "...")] and policies work directly.
* GetArkAccessTokenAsync / WithArkTokenAsync read the current token per call, so a token refreshed
  by the cookie handler is picked up automatically.
* New services for the non-interactive flows: ArkSetupProbe (configuration vs. live metadata),
  ArkClientCredentials (client credentials grant with caching) and ArkRegistration (RFC 7591/7592).

Breaking / migration: the standard flow is now the default. Set ark_oauth_client:UseLegacyFlow to
true to keep the original cookie/bearer middleware while migrating — it does not validate state or
nonce and should be treated as a migration aid, not a supported configuration.

Packaging: the package no longer ships a sample appsettings file into consuming projects, and now
carries a readme, an SPDX license expression and a symbol package.
title: Ark Identity Client — OAuth 2.1 / OpenID Connect for ASP.NET Core
